title: Chain two percentage changes in one line
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Net % change = a + b + (ab / 100)
explanation: For two successive changes of a% and b%, add both changes and then add their product divided by 100. Keep the sign negative for a decrease.
example: A price rises 20% and then falls 10%. Net change = 20 - 10 + (20 x -10)/100 = 8%, so the final price is 8% higher.

title: Convert common percentages to fractions
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
explanation: Memorise the fraction anchors and build nearby percentages by adding or subtracting. This avoids long division in percentage and DI questions.
mnemonic: Halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, then the sevenths and eighths.

title: Use a multiplier instead of profit formulas
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: SP = CP x (100 + profit%) / 100; CP = SP x 100 / (100 + profit%).
explanation: A profit of p% multiplies the cost by (1 + p/100). A loss multiplies it by (1 - l/100). Chain multipliers for successive transactions.

title: Combine two discounts with multipliers
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: SP = MP x (1 - d1/100) x (1 - d2/100); single equivalent = d1 + d2 - d1d2/100.
explanation: Two discounts are not added directly because the second discount applies to the already reduced price. Multiply the retention factors instead.
example: MP = Rs 1000, discounts 20% and 10%. SP = 1000 x 0.8 x 0.9 = Rs 720. Equivalent discount = 28%.

title: Spot the real profit in a rigged weight
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Gain % = Error / (True value - Error) x 100
explanation: When a seller uses a false weight, the customer pays for the claimed weight but receives less. The error is the missing quantity; the cost is what the seller actually gives.
example: A trader uses 900 g instead of 1 kg. Error = 100 g, true value given = 900 g. Gain = 100/900 x 100 = 11.11%.
mnemonic: Error on top, actual goods below.

title: Two-year CI minus SI difference without formulas
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Difference = P x (R / 100)^2
explanation: For two years, the extra amount in compound interest is the interest earned on the first year's interest. That reduces to principal times the square of the rate fraction.

title: Repeated replacement in mixtures
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Final pure = Initial x (1 - replaced / total)^n
explanation: Each replacement removes the same fraction of whatever pure liquid remains. Multiplying that retention fraction n times gives the final pure quantity.
example: 20 L milk, remove 4 L and replace with water, twice. Final milk = 20 x (1 - 4/20)^2 = 20 x 0.64 = 12.8 L.
mnemonic: Keep the fraction, raise it to the number of rounds.

title: Alligation gives the mixing ratio directly
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Ratio = (higher - mean) : (mean - lower)
explanation: Place the two component values on one side and the mean in the middle. Cross-subtract to get the ratio in which the components must be mixed.
example: Mix Rs 40/kg and Rs 60/kg tea to get Rs 45/kg. Ratio = (60 - 45) : (45 - 40) = 15 : 5 = 3 : 1.

title: Average speed when distance is equal
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Average speed = 2xy / (x + y)
explanation: Do not average the two speeds arithmetically. When equal distances are covered at x and y, the total time uses the harmonic mean of the speeds.
example: Go at 40 km/h and return at 60 km/h. Average speed = 2 x 40 x 60 / (40 + 60) = 48 km/h.
mnemonic: Equal distance? Use the harmonic mean.

title: Trains: add speeds for opposite, subtract for same direction
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Time = total length / relative speed; opposite = u + v, same direction = u - v.
explanation: Convert speeds to m/s by multiplying by 5/18 when the length is in metres. A pole has zero length; a platform adds its length.
example: Two 100 m trains at 10 m/s and 15 m/s cross each other in 200 / 25 = 8 s when moving in opposite directions.
mnemonic: Opposite add, same subtract, lengths add.

title: Boat and stream in two equations
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Downstream = b + s; Upstream = b - s; b = (D + U)/2; s = (D - U)/2.
explanation: The stream helps downstream and opposes upstream. Add the two speeds to get twice the boat speed, and subtract to get twice the stream speed.
example: Downstream 18 km/h, upstream 12 km/h. Boat speed = 15 km/h, stream speed = 3 km/h.

title: Take LCM of days as total work
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Total work = LCM of days; efficiency = total work / days.
explanation: Convert each worker's rate into units per day. Then add or subtract efficiencies instead of adding fractions.
example: A does work in 12 days, B in 18 days. LCM = 36 units. A = 3 units/day, B = 2 units/day. Together = 36/5 = 7.2 days.
mnemonic: LCM the days, add the units.

title: Pipes are just positive and negative work
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Net rate = sum of inlet rates - sum of outlet rates.
explanation: Use the same LCM method as time and work. An inlet adds units per hour; an outlet subtracts units per hour.
example: A fills in 6 h, B fills in 12 h, outlet C empties in 18 h. LCM = 36. Net = 6 + 3 - 2 = 7 units/h. Time = 36/7 h.

title: Turn a ratio into parts of the total
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: One share = total / sum of ratio terms; target share = one share x its term.
explanation: Ratios describe parts, not fixed amounts. Add the ratio terms to get the number of equal parts, then multiply by the required term.
example: Rs 1200 divided in 2 : 3. Total parts = 5, one part = 240. A gets 2 x 240 = Rs 480.
mnemonic: Add the parts, divide the total.

title: Average change after adding or replacing a value
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: New average = old average + (new value - old value) / number of items.
explanation: When one item is replaced, only the difference matters. When a new item is added, divide the difference by the new count.
example: Average age of 10 students is 15. A 25-year-old joins. New average = 15 + (25 - 15)/11 = 15.91 years.
mnemonic: Average shifts by the difference spread over the group.

title: LCM x HCF equals the product of two numbers
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: LCM(a, b) x HCF(a, b) = a x b
explanation: This works for exactly two positive integers. If one number and the LCM and HCF are known, the other number is product / known number.
example: HCF = 6, LCM = 72, one number = 24. Other = (6 x 72) / 24 = 18.
mnemonic: Product of numbers equals product of HCF and LCM.

title: Scale length, area and volume separately
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: Length x k -> area x k^2 -> volume x k^3.
explanation: When every dimension is multiplied by k, area grows by the square of k and volume by the cube of k. Use this before calculating exact values.
example: A cube side doubles. Surface area becomes 4 times, volume becomes 8 times.
mnemonic: One dimension, two dimensions, three dimensions.

title: Use the complement for at least one
subject: Quantitative Aptitude
shortcut: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).
explanation: Questions with at least one success are usually faster through the complement. Find the probability that the event never happens, then subtract from 1.
example: A coin is tossed 3 times. P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no head) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.
mnemonic: At least one equals one minus none.

title: Clock angle in five seconds
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Angle = |30H - 5.5M|, then take the smaller angle.
explanation: The hour hand moves 0.5 deg per minute and the minute hand moves 6 deg per minute, so their relative speed is 5.5 deg per minute. The hour hand starts at 30 deg per hour.
example: At 3:20, |30 x 3 - 5.5 x 20| = |90 - 110| = 20 deg. The smaller angle is 20 deg.

title: Count odd days, not full weeks
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Normal year = 1 odd day; leap year = 2; 100 years = 5; 400 years = 0.
explanation: Divide the total days by 7 and keep the remainder. For date questions, add odd days to the starting weekday and wrap around Sunday to Monday.
example: If today is Monday, after 100 days: 100 mod 7 = 2, so the day is Wednesday.

title: Reverse only the negative quantifier
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: No A is B -> No B is A; Some A is B -> Some B is A; All A is B does not reverse.
explanation: Universal positive statements are not reversible unless the set sizes are identical. Particular positive and universal negative statements are reversible.
example: All pens are tools does not imply all tools are pens. But No pen is a tool does imply no tool is a pen.
mnemonic: All stays forward; No and Some can turn around.

title: Build a generation ladder for blood relations
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Put every person on a generation line: +1 up, -1 down, 0 same generation.
explanation: Convert each relation into a generation jump and a gender marker. Then trace the target person from the speaker instead of trying to hold the whole family tree in memory.
example: A's father's sister is A's aunt. Father = +1, sister = 0, so aunt is +1 generation with female gender.
mnemonic: Jump, mark gender, then walk the ladder.

title: Turn directions on a fixed compass
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Right turn: N -> E -> S -> W -> N. Left turn: N -> W -> S -> E -> N.
explanation: Draw the start point and move one segment at a time. At the end, use Pythagoras for distance and compare the final x and y signs for direction.
example: Walk 3 km north, turn right, walk 4 km east. Distance from start = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 km, north-east.
mnemonic: Right follows the clock; left goes back.

title: Ranking from both ends
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Total = rank from top + rank from bottom - 1.
explanation: The person is counted twice, once from each end, so subtract one. Rearrange the same formula to find an unknown rank.
example: A is 7th from top and 12th from bottom. Total = 7 + 12 - 1 = 18 students.
mnemonic: Add both ranks, subtract the overlap.

title: Lock the alphabet pairs and EJOTY
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Opposite pairs sum to 27: A-Z, B-Y, C-X. EJOTY = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
explanation: Use opposite pairs for reverse-alphabet questions and EJOTY for quick position lookup. Count from the nearer end if the letter is late in the alphabet.
example: 15th letter from left is O. 12th from right = 26 - 12 + 1 = 15, also O.
mnemonic: Pairs make 27; EJOTY marks the fives.

title: Crack letter codes by measuring the shift
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Compare first letters, find the shift, then check if the shift is constant, increasing or reversed.
explanation: Write alphabet positions under the letters. The difference between the code and the word usually reveals a fixed or patterned shift.
example: CAT -> DBU means each letter moved +1. DOG -> EPH.

title: Check differences before guessing a series
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Try first differences, second differences, ratios, squares, cubes and alternating patterns.
explanation: A constant first difference means an arithmetic series. A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern. Ratios reveal geometric or factorial patterns.
example: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? Differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12 and the answer is 42.

title: Name the relationship before choosing an option
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: State the first pair as a short sentence, then apply the same sentence to the second pair.
explanation: Common relationships are worker-place, tool-action, cause-effect, part-whole, young-adult and synonym-antonym. Naming the link prevents attractive but wrong options.
example: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : School, because the first works in the second.
mnemonic: Make a sentence, match the sentence.

title: Classify the group before finding the odd one
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Check the common property: number type, prime, square, cube, living-nonliving, metal, currency, capital.
explanation: Three options usually share a precise property and one does not. Test the most specific property first, not the broadest category.
example: 4, 9, 16, 25, 30. All except 30 are perfect squares.
mnemonic: Find the rule that exactly three obey.

title: Combine inequalities in one direction
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: A > B > C means A > C. Reverse the sign when reading right to left.
explanation: Keep the chain pointing the same way. A conclusion is definitely true only if the chain directly connects the two elements with the same strict or non-strict sign.
example: A > B >= C = D implies A > D, but does not imply D > A.
mnemonic: Follow the arrow; reverse flips it.

title: Painted cube counts for 3 x 3 x 3
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: 3 x 3 x 3: 1 with no paint, 6 with one face, 12 with two faces, 8 with three faces.
explanation: The unpainted cube is the hidden centre. One-face cubes sit at face centres, two-face cubes on edges, and three-face cubes at corners.
example: A 3 x 3 x 3 painted cube is cut into 27 small cubes. Exactly 6 small cubes have one painted face.

title: Standard dice opposite faces add to seven
subject: Reasoning
shortcut: Opposite pairs: 1-6, 2-5, 3-4. Opposite faces never appear together in one view.
explanation: Use the sum-to-seven rule for a standard die. For non-standard dice, eliminate adjacent faces from two views to find the opposite face.
example: If 3 is on top of a standard die, 4 is at the bottom.

title: Since a point, for a duration
subject: English
shortcut: Since + starting point; For + length of time.
explanation: Use since with a specific point in time (since 2019, since Monday) and for with a period (for three years, for two hours).
example: She has lived here since 2019. She has lived here for five years.

title: Choose articles by sound, not spelling
subject: English
shortcut: A before a consonant sound, an before a vowel sound, the for something specific or unique.
explanation: Look at the first sound of the next word. An hour starts with a vowel sound; a university starts with a consonant sound.
example: An honest man, a European country, the Ganga.

title: Find the real subject before the verb
subject: English
shortcut: Each, every, either, neither and everyone are singular; either/or and neither/nor follow the nearer subject.
explanation: Prepositional phrases between the subject and verb do not change the verb. Identify the head noun first, then apply the agreement rule.
example: Each of the students is ready. Neither the teacher nor the students were informed.
mnemonic: Cross out the phrase, then match the verb.

title: Decode one-word substitutions with roots
subject: English
shortcut: Learn the root, not the whole word: -cide = killing, -phobia = fear, -logy = study, -ocracy = rule.
explanation: One-word substitution questions often reuse Greek or Latin roots. Recognising the root narrows four options to one even when the full word is unfamiliar.
example: Homicide = killing of a human; xenophobia = fear of foreigners; democracy = rule by the people.

title: Test synonyms inside the original sentence
subject: English
shortcut: Replace the word with each option and keep the sentence meaning and tone unchanged.
explanation: A synonym must fit the context, not just share a dictionary meaning. Check whether the option is too strong, too weak or has the wrong connotation.
example: The evidence was abundant means plentiful, not rare or brief.

title: Use prefixes to spot antonyms
subject: English
shortcut: Negative prefixes: un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, non-, mis-.
explanation: Many antonyms are formed by adding a negative prefix. Check whether the option is a direct opposite rather than a related word.
example: Possible -> impossible; legal -> illegal; honest -> dishonest.

title: Read idioms as one fixed unit
subject: English
shortcut: Never translate an idiom word by word; learn the figurative meaning as a phrase.
explanation: Idioms have a fixed meaning that is different from the literal words. Group them by theme such as effort, secrecy, difficulty or honesty.
example: Break the ice means start a conversation, not break frozen water.

title: Spot the double-letter traps
subject: English
shortcut: Accommodation has double c and double m; committee has double m, double t and double e.
explanation: Learn spelling by letter clusters and common traps. Say the word in syllables and mark the doubled letters visually.
example: Necessary has one c and double s. Occurrence has double c, double r and double e.
mnemonic: Mark the doubles before you choose.

title: Convert active to passive in three moves
subject: English
shortcut: Object becomes subject, verb becomes past participle, subject becomes by-agent.
explanation: Keep the tense of the original verb. Use the correct form of be plus the past participle. Drop the agent when it is unknown or unimportant.
example: The teacher teaches the students -> The students are taught by the teacher.
mnemonic: Object first, third form second, by-agent last.

title: Find the opening sentence by its links
subject: English
shortcut: Look for the sentence with no unexplained pronoun, then follow pronouns, connectors and chronology.
explanation: A pronoun usually refers to a noun in an earlier sentence. Connectors such as however, therefore and moreover reveal the logical flow. Dates and sequence words set the order.
example: A sentence starting with This decision must follow the sentence that describes the decision.
mnemonic: No orphan pronoun in the opening.

title: Lock the Finance Commission article
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: Finance Commission = Article 280; it is constituted every five years.
explanation: Article 280 requires the President to constitute a Finance Commission every five years to recommend distribution of taxes between the Union and the States.
example: A question asks which article creates the Finance Commission. Answer: Article 280, not 275 or 315.

title: Frame the Fundamental Rights range
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: Fundamental Rights: Articles 12 to 35, six categories.
explanation: Part III contains the Fundamental Rights. Article 12 defines the State, Article 13 protects against inconsistent laws, and Articles 14 to 32 cover the six rights; Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies.
example: Right to Equality starts at Article 14. Right to Constitutional Remedies is Article 32, called the heart and soul of the Constitution by Dr Ambedkar.

title: Anchor the four most asked articles
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: 14 = equality, 19 = freedoms, 21 = life and liberty, 32 = writ remedies.
explanation: These four articles appear repeatedly in polity questions. Pair each number with one keyword and one remedy or right.
example: Habeas corpus is a writ under Article 32. Equality before law is Article 14.

title: Cluster modern history dates
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: 1857 revolt, 1885 Congress, 1905 partition of Bengal, 1919 Jallianwala and Rowlatt, 1930 Dandi, 1942 Quit India, 1947 independence, 1950 Constitution.
explanation: Attach one event to each date and arrange them on a timeline. Questions often ask what came before or after a given event.
example: The Quit India Movement came after the Dandi March: 1942 after 1930.

title: Group Indian rivers by direction
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: West-flowing: Narmada and Tapi. East-flowing: Ganga, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
explanation: Most major peninsular rivers flow east into the Bay of Bengal. Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea.
example: The Narmada flows west, while the Godavari flows east.
mnemonic: Narmada and Tapi go against the eastern crowd.

title: Match quantity to SI unit
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: Force = newton, work = joule, power = watt, pressure = pascal, frequency = hertz.
explanation: Link the unit to the formula. Work is force times distance, power is work per second, and pressure is force per area.
example: The SI unit of power is the watt, not the joule.
mnemonic: Force N, work J, power W, pressure Pa, frequency Hz.

title: Pair vitamins with deficiency diseases
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: A = night blindness, B1 = beriberi, C = scurvy, D = rickets, K = poor clotting.
explanation: Vitamins are asked as direct pairs. Learn the vitamin letter, its chemical name and one deficiency disease together.
example: Scurvy is caused by Vitamin C deficiency, not Vitamin D.
mnemonic: A eyes, B1 nerves, C gums, D bones, K clotting.

title: Keep GDP and GST basics straight
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). GST was launched in 2017 as a destination-based indirect tax.
explanation: GDP measures final goods and services produced within a country in a year. GST replaced many indirect taxes and is levied at the point of consumption.
example: If exports exceed imports, net exports are positive and add to GDP.

title: Group the firsts of independent India
subject: General Awareness
shortcut: First President Rajendra Prasad, first PM Nehru, first Governor-General Mountbatten, first woman PM Indira Gandhi.
explanation: Static firsts are easy marks when grouped by office. Keep the office and the person together, not as isolated names.
example: C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General, not the first.

title: Lock the everyday computer shortcuts
subject: Computer Awareness
shortcut: Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+P print.
explanation: Shortcut questions are direct recall. Group them by action: clipboard, editing, file and window control.
example: Ctrl+Z undoes the last action; Ctrl+Y redoes it.
mnemonic: C copy, V paste, X cut, Z back, Y forward.

title: Walk through computer generations
subject: Computer Awareness
shortcut: 1 vacuum tubes, 2 transistors, 3 integrated circuits, 4 microprocessors, 5 artificial intelligence.
explanation: Each generation is defined by its core hardware technology. Attach the technology to the generation number and one example.
example: Third-generation computers used integrated circuits, not vacuum tubes.

title: Climb the memory units
subject: Computer Awareness
shortcut: 8 bits = 1 byte; KB, MB, GB and TB each usually step by 1024.
explanation: Bit is the smallest unit. Byte is eight bits. Storage questions often ask for the order or the number of bits in a byte.
example: 1 KB = 1024 bytes in binary storage convention.

title: Match internet protocols to their job
subject: Computer Awareness
shortcut: HTTP/HTTPS = web, FTP = file transfer, SMTP = sending mail, DNS = name to IP, TCP/IP = core internet.
explanation: Protocols are named by function. Learn the full form and one action for each instead of memorising a long list.
example: DNS converts a domain name such as example.com into an IP address.

title: Separate the four database keys
subject: Computer Awareness
shortcut: Primary = chosen unique key; candidate = any unique key; foreign = links tables; composite = made of multiple columns.
explanation: A table can have several candidate keys but only one primary key. A foreign key references a key in another table.
example: Roll number can be the primary key; student email can be a candidate key; class id can be a foreign key.
mnemonic: Primary chosen, candidate possible, foreign linked, composite combined.

title: Remember RBI by its five hats
subject: Banking Awareness
shortcut: RBI is note issuer, banker to government, banker to banks, lender of last resort, and monetary authority.
explanation: The RBI performs several roles at once. Group them as issue, government, banks, emergency support and policy.
example: The RBI issues currency notes except one-rupee notes and coins, which are issued by the Government of India.

title: Sort the monetary policy tools
subject: Banking Awareness
shortcut: Repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, MSF and open market operations are the main tools.
explanation: Repo is the rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to banks. Reverse repo absorbs liquidity. CRR and SLR are reserve requirements.
example: To inject liquidity, RBI can cut CRR or buy government securities through OMO.

title: NPA in one threshold and three tools
subject: Banking Awareness
shortcut: Loan overdue for 90 days = NPA; recovery tools include SARFAESI, DRT and IBC.
explanation: An asset becomes non-performing when the borrower stops servicing interest or principal for 90 days. Gross NPA is before provisions; net NPA is after provisions.
example: A term loan unpaid for more than 90 days is classified as an NPA.

title: IFSC and MICR by length
subject: Banking Awareness
shortcut: IFSC = 11 characters; MICR = 9 digits.
explanation: IFSC identifies a bank branch for electronic transfers. MICR is printed on cheques for faster clearing. The first four IFSC characters identify the bank.
example: An IFSC code starts with four letters, followed by 0 and a six-character branch code.
mnemonic: Eleven for IFSC, nine for MICR.

title: Cover the priority sector categories
subject: Banking Awareness
shortcut: Priority sectors include agriculture, MSME, education, housing, export credit and weaker sections.
explanation: Banks must allocate a minimum share of lending to priority sectors. The overall target is 40% of adjusted net bank credit for domestic commercial banks.
example: A small farmer's crop loan and a micro-enterprise loan both count under priority sector lending.
mnemonic: Farm, small business, study, home, export, weaker sections.

title: Order Piaget's four stages
subject: Teaching Aptitude
shortcut: Sensorimotor 0-2, pre-operational 2-7, concrete operational 7-11, formal operational 11+.
explanation: Each stage adds a new thinking ability. Conservation appears in the concrete operational stage; abstract hypothetical reasoning appears in the formal stage.
example: A child who understands that water volume stays the same across differently shaped glasses is in the concrete operational stage.

title: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
subject: Teaching Aptitude
shortcut: ZPD = what a learner can do with guidance but not alone; scaffolding is the temporary support that is removed.
explanation: Vygotsky emphasised social interaction and guided learning. The teacher provides support at the edge of the learner's current ability and gradually fades it.
example: A teacher gives sentence starters for a paragraph, then removes them as the student becomes independent.
mnemonic: ZPD is the gap; scaffolding is the bridge.

title: Climb Bloom's revised taxonomy
subject: Teaching Aptitude
shortcut: Remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create.
explanation: The revised taxonomy moves from lower-order recall to higher-order creation. Questions often ask for the correct order or the highest level in an activity.
example: Designing a new experiment is at the create level, not the remember level.

title: Place formative, summative and diagnostic
subject: Teaching Aptitude
shortcut: Diagnostic before, formative during, summative at the end.
explanation: Diagnostic assessment finds learning gaps before teaching. Formative assessment monitors progress during learning. Summative assessment measures achievement at the end.
example: A short quiz in the middle of a lesson is formative; the annual examination is summative.

title: Inclusion means common classroom, different support
subject: Teaching Aptitude
shortcut: Inclusive education = all learners in the same classroom with accommodations, not segregation.
explanation: Inclusion responds to learner diversity by adapting teaching, materials and assessment. It does not mean giving every learner identical instruction.
example: A student with low vision uses enlarged text and an audio version while learning with peers.

title: NDA maths formula starters
subject: Defence Exams
shortcut: sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1; speed = distance / time; area of triangle = 1/2 x base x height.
explanation: NDA maths rewards fast recall of core identities and standard formulas. Revise trigonometry, algebra, mensuration and coordinate geometry in short formula blocks.
example: If sin A = 3/5, then cos A = 4/5 in a right triangle with hypotenuse 5.
mnemonic: Identity, speed, area: three marks in three seconds.

title: NDA GAT is static plus science plus current
subject: Defence Exams
shortcut: Divide GAT revision into static GK, general science, history, geography and current affairs.
explanation: The General Ability Test is broad but shallow. Use one-page fact sheets and eliminate extreme options. Do not spend too long on a single static question.
example: A question on the capital of a country should be answered in seconds or skipped for later.

title: Know the Agniveer GD paper pattern
subject: Defence Exams
shortcut: Agniveer GD: 50 questions, 100 marks, 60 minutes, 0.25 negative marking.
explanation: The paper covers general knowledge, science, maths and reasoning. Because the time is tight, attempt easy factual and arithmetic questions first.
example: A direct science fact is a better first attempt than a long calculation.
mnemonic: Fifty questions, one hour, small negative.

title: Know your negative-marking break-even
subject: Exam Strategy
shortcut: Break-even accuracy = negative / (marks + negative). For 0.25 negative, it is 20%; for 0.33, it is 25%; for 0.5, it is 33.3%.
explanation: If your true accuracy on a question type is above the break-even point, guessing has positive expected value. If it is below, leave it.
example: With 1 mark for correct and 0.25 for wrong, a guess needs more than 20% accuracy to be worth it.

title: Eliminate before you calculate
subject: Exam Strategy
shortcut: Remove absurd, extreme and unit-mismatched options first; then use parity, approximation and option substitution.
explanation: Many MCQs can be solved by narrowing the choices. Check the last digit, rough magnitude, sign and units before doing the full calculation.
example: If the answer must be a percentage below 100, eliminate options above 100 immediately.

title: Turn every mock into a review loop
subject: Exam Strategy
shortcut: After each mock: 20-minute review, classify errors as concept, calculation, time or guess, then reattempt the same paper after two days.
explanation: The score is feedback, not the final goal. A short review that names the error type creates a specific fix for the next attempt.
example: Three wrong questions from the same topic become one revision block, not three separate regrets.

title: GATE negative marking: know which questions can hurt
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: GATE MCQ: -1/3 for a 1-mark question and -2/3 for a 2-mark question. MSQ and NAT have no negative marking.
explanation: Never guess an MCQ unless you can eliminate options. MSQ and NAT are safer for calculated attempts because a wrong answer does not reduce your score.
example: A blind guess on a 2-mark MCQ costs 0.67 marks when wrong; a blind NAT guess costs nothing but rarely helps.
mnemonic: MCQ only: one-third or two-thirds down.

title: Cache AMAT in one line
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty.
explanation: Convert every term to the same unit, then multiply the miss rate by the full miss penalty. TLB and page-table questions use the same structure.
example: Hit time 2 ns, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 80 ns: AMAT = 2 + 0.05 x 80 = 6 ns.
mnemonic: Hit plus miss fraction times penalty.

title: Page offset bits from page size
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Page offset bits = log2(page size in bytes). Virtual page number bits = virtual address bits - offset bits.
explanation: Powers of two make this instant. For 4 KB pages the offset is 12 bits; for 32-bit addresses the VPN is 20 bits.
example: 4 KB = 2^12, so a 32-bit virtual address has 12 offset bits and 20 VPN bits.
mnemonic: Offset is the log of page size.

title: Climb the normal-form ladder
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependency. 3NF: no transitive dependency. BCNF: every determinant is a superkey.
explanation: Check the ladder in order. If a relation fails 1NF, higher normal forms are not meaningful until repeating groups are removed.
example: A non-key attribute depending on part of a composite key violates 2NF, not 3NF.

title: Pipeline speedup without stalls
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: For n instructions and k stages, speedup = n x k / (k + n - 1). As n grows, it approaches k.
explanation: The first instruction takes k cycles and each additional instruction takes one cycle. This ignores stalls, hazards and unequal stage delays.
example: For a 5-stage pipeline and a very large n, ideal speedup approaches 5.
mnemonic: Fill the pipe once, then one per cycle.

title: MSQ is a set-matching game
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: For MSQ, compare the selected set with the correct set exactly. Missing one correct option or adding one wrong option makes the answer wrong.
explanation: There is no partial credit. Treat each option as an independent true/false statement, then verify that every true statement is selected.
example: If the correct set is {A, C, D} and you select {A, C}, the answer is wrong even though two choices match.

title: Check pigeonhole before counting cases
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: If n objects go into k boxes and n > k, some box contains at least 2 objects. For a guaranteed r in one box, use ceil(n/k).
explanation: The pigeonhole principle proves existence without listing arrangements. Keep the distinction between a lower bound and an exact count.
example: Among 13 integers, two have the same remainder modulo 12.
mnemonic: Objects over boxes; round up for the guarantee.

title: Use the handshake lemma first
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Sum of degrees = 2|E|. In a tree, |E| = |V| - 1. A connected graph needs at least |V| - 1 edges.
explanation: Every undirected edge contributes one degree at each endpoint. A degree sum must therefore be even, which is a quick consistency check.
example: Degree sum 18 means 9 edges; a tree with 10 vertices also has 9 edges.

title: Prove binary search with an invariant
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: At each iteration, keep the target inside the candidate interval. Each comparison halves its size, so comparisons are O(log2 n).
explanation: Check loop boundaries separately for inclusive and half-open intervals. Most off-by-one errors come from changing one convention mid-proof.
example: For 1024 sorted items, at most about 10 halvings isolate one item.
mnemonic: State the interval, preserve it, halve it.

title: Compare n to the recursion work
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). Smaller: recursion dominates. Same order: add a log n factor. Larger: f(n) dominates when regularity holds.
explanation: Verify the regularity condition in the larger-work case and check whether f(n) is polynomially larger. The shortcut does not cover every recurrence.
example: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n has n^(log2 2)=n, so T(n)=Theta(n log n).

title: Minimize a DFA by distinguishable pairs
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Mark every final/non-final pair first. Then mark a pair if some input sends it to an already marked pair; repeat until stable.
explanation: Unmarked states are equivalent and can be merged. A distinguishing suffix is a certificate that two states must remain separate.
example: If input 0 sends states p and q to a final/non-final pair, p and q are distinguishable.
mnemonic: Different acceptance first, then propagate backward.

title: Check CNF productions before CYK
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: For strict CNF, productions are A → BC or A → a, with S → epsilon allowed only when the language includes epsilon and S is handled specially.
explanation: Convert unit and epsilon productions carefully before using CYK. A missing start-symbol exception can change whether epsilon is generated.
example: CYK for a string of length n fills triangular cells and checks O(n^3) split positions for a fixed grammar.

title: Build FIRST and FOLLOW in two passes
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: FIRST asks what can begin a derivation. FOLLOW asks what may appear immediately after a nonterminal; put $ in FOLLOW(start).
explanation: Propagate epsilon through a sequence from left to right. Add FOLLOW(lhs) to FOLLOW(B) only when the suffix after B can derive epsilon.
example: For A → Bc, add c to FOLLOW(B); for A → B, add FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B).

title: Find keys with attribute closure
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Start with X+ = X and repeatedly apply dependencies whose left side is contained in X+. X is a superkey when X+ contains every attribute.
explanation: To prove a candidate key, show it is a superkey and that removing each attribute makes it fail. A superkey alone need not be minimal.
example: For A → B and B → C, A+ = {A,B,C}, so A is a candidate key if no proper subset determines all attributes.
mnemonic: Close, cover, then remove one at a time.

title: Test deadlock safety with available work
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Find a process whose remaining need is <= available. Pretend it finishes, return its allocation to available, and repeat.
explanation: A complete ordering is a safe sequence. If the scan gets stuck, that state is unsafe; it does not by itself prove a deadlock already exists.
example: Compare each Need vector component-wise against Available before selecting a process.

title: Read subnet size from the prefix
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: IPv4 addresses per prefix /p = 2^(32-p). Traditional usable hosts are 2^(32-p)-2, except special point-to-point and boundary cases.
explanation: The prefix gives network bits; the remaining bits identify addresses within that block. Check whether the question asks total addresses or usable host addresses.
example: /26 leaves 6 host bits: 64 total addresses, usually 62 usable hosts.

title: Check signed range before arithmetic
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: An n-bit two's-complement integer ranges from -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1. Overflow occurs when same-sign operands produce a result with the opposite sign.
explanation: Carry out of the sign bit alone is not the signed overflow test. Use operand and result signs, or XOR the carry into and out of the sign bit.
example: In 8 bits, 127 + 1 wraps to -128 and signals signed overflow.
mnemonic: Same signs in, changed sign out: overflow.

title: Split cache address into tag, index, offset
subject: GATE CSE
shortcut: Offset bits = log2(block bytes). For a set-associative cache, index bits = log2(number of sets). Tag bits = address bits - index bits - offset bits.
explanation: Convert capacity and associativity to number of sets first. State byte versus word address assumptions before subtracting bit fields.
example: A 32 KB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks has 128 sets and 6 offset bits, so index uses 7 bits.
